content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued several recommendations aimed at improving outcomes for preterm and low birth weight infants. These include interventions to enhance preterm birth outcomes, management of common childhood conditions such as pneumonia, dysentery, and severe acute malnutrition, and the use of oxygen therapy. Evidence-based interventions for preterm or low birth weight infants have been systematically reviewed, including the benefits of kangaroo mother care (KMC), which has been shown to improve survival rates. Studies have explored barriers and enablers to the adoption of KMC in healthcare systems, as well as its implementation in resource-limited settings. Research has also highlighted the importance of skin-to-skin care and breastfeeding in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs), emphasizing the role of parental involvement. Nutritional management for preterm infants has been extensively studied, with a focus on optimal feeding practices, including the use of human milk, formula, and donor breast milk. Fortification of breast milk with essential nutrients such as fat, protein, and carbohydrates is recommended to support growth and development. Micronutrient supplementation, including iron, zinc, and vitamin D, has been evaluated for its role in preventing morbidity and mortality in preterm infants. Probiotics have also been investigated for their potential to prevent necrotizing enterocolitis and sepsis, though concerns about safety and strain-specific effects remain. The development of the newborn epidermis and the use of topical emollients to prevent infections in preterm infants have been studied, highlighting the increased vulnerability of preterm newborns to infections due to their underdeveloped skin barrier. These findings underscore the importance of evidence-based practices in neonatal care to improve health outcomes for this vulnerable population.
